findings.claim: Every lesson's first practice question reads 'Give two things you can learn from Source A' (also in the L1 exam tip).
findings.truth: Paper 3 Question 1 asks what you can INFER from the source. 'What can you learn' is not the stem this paper sets; the inference wording is what the mark scheme rewards.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information - Q1 'targets AO3, and focuses on making inferences from a source'

findings.claim: The 'Explain why' question is labelled '8 marks - Explain Why' in all ten lessons, with bands 7-8 / 5-6 / 3-4 / 1-2. Exam tips in lessons 1, 2 and 6 repeat '(8 marks)'.
findings.truth: Paper 3 Section A is 16 marks over two questions: the 4-mark inference question and the causation question, so 'Explain why' is 12 marks. Bands rebuilt as 10-12 / 7-9 / 4-6 / 1-3. The 8-mark label also routed these answers to the short-answer AI marker (js/main.js reads the first number in q.type).
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information - Section A 'is marked out of 16', Q1 inference + Q2 causation; Section B 8+4+4+(16+4)=36 confirms the pattern

findings.claim: In lessons 1-5 the 16+4 question is a statement with stimulus bullets: "'...' How far do you agree? ... You may use the following in your answer: ...". Lesson 4's exam tip describes it the same way.
findings.truth: That is the Paper 1 thematic-study form. On Paper 3 the 16+4 question evaluates one of the two interpretations printed on the paper, using the other interpretation and contextual knowledge; it carries no stimulus bullets. Rewritten to the interpretation form used correctly in lessons 6-10.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information - Q3(d) 'requires students to evaluate one interpretation, making use of the other interpretation and their knowledge of the historical context'

findings.claim: Every lesson's fourth question reads 'How do Interpretations 1 and 2 differ about ...?', labelled '4 marks - How Do Interpretations Differ'.
findings.truth: That is the AQA stem. Paper 3 Question 3(b) asks for the main difference between the two views, explained from details in both interpretations. Stem and label converted.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information - Q3(b) 'uses two later written interpretations. Students explain how the two interpretations differ'

findings.claim: 'This kind of linked reasoning is what moves you from Level 2 to Level 3 and beyond'.
findings.truth: 'Level 2' / 'Level 3' are banned band names - the validator rejects the whole unit. Rewritten with the house band vocabulary.
findings.evidence: checker brief, banned strings

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward students who show understanding of significance'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as a statement about what top-band answers do.
findings.evidence: checker brief - invented exam claims are removed

findings.claim: Lessons 6-10, first question: '1 marks for each valid inference supported by detail from the source (max 2 inferences, 2 marks each)'.
findings.truth: Self-contradictory answer key. It is 1 mark for the inference and 1 mark for the supporting detail, twice, for 4 marks.
findings.evidence: spec, Paper 3 assessment information

findings.claim: 'The winter of 1917-18 became known as the "Turnip Winter"' (repeated in a flashcard and in the lesson-1 mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Steckruebenwinter was the winter of 1916-17.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Turnip Winter'; the already-checked AQA Germany unit in this programme uses 1916-17

findings.claim: 'In late October 1918, German sailors at Kiel mutinied'; 'On 29 October 1918, naval commanders ordered the German fleet to sail from Kiel'; 'the authorities arrested around 1,000 sailors'. Repeated in the timeline, the match set, a flashcard and the mark scheme.
findings.truth: The order to sail was refused at Wilhelmshaven on 29-30 October 1918. The Kiel mutiny itself began on 3 November and the city was in the sailors' hands by 4 November, when about 40,000 sailors, soldiers and workers controlled it. The arrest figure of about 1,000 is not supported; roughly 150-200 were held.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kiel mutiny' - 3-11 November 1918; same correction already made in the AQA Germany unit (F10 there)

findings.claim: '9 different chancellors in 14 years' (lesson 1 mark scheme); '28 coalition governments in 14 years' (lesson 4 content and mark scheme).
findings.truth: Twelve individuals held the chancellorship between February 1919 and 30 January 1933, across twenty cabinets. Both figures replaced with the chancellor count.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'List of chancellors of Germany' - 12 distinct individuals in the Weimar period

findings.claim: Reichstag defined as 'The German parliament, consisting of the Reichstag (elected lower house) and the Reichsrat (upper house...)'.
findings.truth: The definition defines the term as containing itself. The Reichstag is the elected lower house; the Reichsrat represented the states.
findings.evidence: Weimar Constitution, Articles 20-22 and 60-63

findings.claim: 'the Polish Corridor and Upper Silesia given to Poland'.
findings.truth: Versailles ordered a plebiscite in Upper Silesia (March 1921); only the eastern industrial part went to Poland, in 1922. Versailles itself did not hand it over.
findings.evidence: Treaty of Versailles, Articles 88 and annex

findings.claim: 'President Ebert used the Freikorps' during the Spartacist uprising of January 1919.
findings.truth: Ebert was head of the provisional government (chairman of the Council of People's Representatives) in January 1919. He was elected President on 11 February 1919. Changed to 'Ebert's government'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Friedrich Ebert' - elected Reichspraesident 11 February 1919

findings.claim: Wolfgang Kapp described as 'a right-wing journalist'.
findings.truth: Kapp was a Prussian civil servant and nationalist politician (doctorate in law 1886, Prussian Finance Ministry, director of the East Prussian Agricultural Credit Institute, Reichstag member 1918).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Wolfgang Kapp'

findings.claim: Flashcard 'In January ____, a loaf of bread cost 0.63 marks; by November ____ it cost ____ billion marks.' with the answer '1921 / 1923 / 200.'
findings.truth: A three-blank question with a slash-separated answer breaks the one-idea-per-card rule and the validator's no-list-answer rule. Rewritten as a single-idea card about the November 1923 price.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: 'In January 1921, a loaf of bread cost 0.63 marks' (also in the key fact and the conclusion).
findings.truth: 0.63 marks is the opening row of the bread-price table used in GCSE textbooks, and that row is normally dated 1918, not January 1921. The rest of the series in the lesson (250 marks January 1923, 1.5 million September 1923, 200 billion November 1923) matches that table exactly, and Wikipedia confirms its 1922 row (about 160 marks at the end of 1922). I could not verify the 0.63 row's date from an approved source, so I have not edited it. Options: (a) redate to 1918, (b) drop the date and say 'just after the war', (c) leave. Recommend (a).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic' - about 160 marks at the end of 1922, 200 billion by late 1923; no row for 0.63
findings.ruling: Redated to 1918 per the standard table.

findings.claim: 'American banks loaned $800 million to Germany' (repeated in the glossary, the Dawes Plan definition, a knowledge check, a flashcard and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The Dawes Plan loan was 800 million marks (about $200 million), roughly half of it raised through Wall Street bond issues. Stating it in dollars inflates the sum four-fold.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Dawes Plan' - 'Germany was loaned 800 million Reichsmarks ... about half of the sum was raised through Wall Street bond issues'

findings.claim: 'In March 1932, Hitler stood against ... Hindenburg. Hindenburg won with 53% of the vote, but Hitler gained ... 36.8%'. Repeated in the timeline and a flashcard.
findings.truth: 53.0% and 36.8% are the figures for the second round, held on 10 April 1932. In the March first round Hindenburg took 49.6% and Hitler 30.1%; no candidate won a majority, which is why a run-off was needed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1932 German presidential election'

findings.claim: Flashcard 'The ____ Revolt of 1917 made German middle classes fear communism.' with the answer 'Russian'.
findings.truth: It was the Russian Revolution, not a 'Revolt', and a one-word answer to a blank fails the flashcard rules. Rewritten as a 'Which event' question with a full answer.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: 'Conservative politician who scheming led to Hitler becoming Chancellor.'
findings.truth: Broken sentence - 'whose scheming'.

findings.claim: 'the SS arrested and executed Roehm and at least 85 other SA leaders'.
findings.truth: At least 85 people were killed in the purge in total, and they were not all SA leaders - von Schleicher, Gregor Strasser and von Kahr were among the dead. The lesson's own glossary gives the figure correctly. Roehm was arrested on 30 June and shot on 1 July 1934.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Night of the Long Knives' - at least 85 killed; the lesson's own glossary entry

findings.claim: 'In Cologne in 1944, twelve Edelweiss Pirates were publicly hanged.'
findings.truth: Thirteen members of the Ehrenfeld group were publicly hanged in Cologne in November 1944, six of them teenagers connected to the Pirates.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Edelweiss Pirates' - 'a group of thirteen people ... were publicly hanged in Cologne'

findings.claim: 'Who initially held in Nazi concentration camps?' answered 'Political prisoners - Communists, Social Democrats, trade unionists, critics.'
findings.truth: Broken question, and the answer is a bare comma list, which the validator rejects.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: 'After Kristallnacht, around 250,000 Jewish people fled Germany'. Repeated in a flashcard.
findings.truth: About 282,000 Jewish people left Germany across the whole period 1933-39. In the ten months after Kristallnacht the figure was roughly 100,000. The 250,000 claim reads like the whole-period total misattributed to the months after November 1938.
findings.evidence: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia 'German Jewish refugees, 1933-1939' - about 282,000 left Germany by September 1939; 36,000 left in 1938 and 77,000 in 1939

findings.claim: 'Subsidised holidays, theatre trips, sporting events and cruises.' and 'Roma and Sinti (also: Slavs, homosexuals, disabled people).' - the latter answering 'Name ONE group'.
findings.truth: Bare comma-list answers; the second also answers a one-item question with four items.
findings.evidence: checker brief, flashcard rules

findings.claim: Kristallnacht: 'over 1,000 synagogues ... 7,500 Jewish businesses ... around 30,000 Jewish men ... At least 91 Jewish people were killed'.
findings.truth: Within the range of scholarship and matched to what GCSE textbooks teach. The USHMM article now gives 'more than 1,400 synagogues', 'about 26,000 Jewish men' and 'hundreds died'. The lesson's figures are conservative rather than wrong, so left alone.
findings.evidence: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia 'Kristallnacht'

findings.claim: 'The Gestapo had around 32,000 officers for a country of 66 million people.'
findings.truth: Published figures run from about 20,000 to about 32,000 depending on year and on whether clerical staff are counted. Not wrong; left alone.

findings.claim: 'the birth rate ... from 15.1 per thousand in 1933 to 20.4 per thousand in 1939'.
findings.truth: Most tables give 14.7 for 1933 with 20.4 for 1939. I could not settle the 1933 figure from an approved source, so it is left as it stands.

findings.claim: 'He served as a corporal in the German army'.
findings.truth: Hitler's rank was Gefreiter, closer to lance corporal. 'Corporal' is the standard textbook rendering and costs no marks; left alone.

findings.claim: 'Roehm ... commanded over 3 million Brownshirts'.
findings.truth: Estimates for SA strength in 1934 run from about 2.5 million to over 4 million. Not wrong; left alone.

findings.claim: 'Between 1924 and 1929, Germany received around $3 billion in loans and investment from the United States.'
findings.truth: Textbooks more often give the sum in marks (about 25 billion by 1930). The dollar figure is within the range of published estimates, so it is left; only the Dawes loan itself was clearly wrong (F17).

summary: Ten lessons checked. The narrative history is in good order - dates, election results, treaty terms and the 1933-34 consolidation are almost all right. The damage is in the exam furniture: the whole unit taught the 12-mark 'Explain why' as an 8-mark question, used the AQA stems for Q1 and Q3(b), and set the 16+4 question in the Paper 1 thematic form in half the lessons. Seven factual errors carry marks - the Turnip Winter, the Kiel mutiny date, the Dawes loan in dollars, the 1932 presidential figures, the chancellor counts, the Night of the Long Knives death toll and the post-Kristallnacht emigration figure. One banned band name ('Level 2') would have failed the validator on its own.
